title: The German Pilot Who Let a Bomber Go
text:
On December 20, 1943, an American B-17 bomber nicknamed Ye Olde Pub, piloted by 21 year old Charles Brown, was badly shot up over Bremen, Germany. One engine was dead, much of the tail was shot away, one crewman was dead and several were wounded. It limped west alone.

A German fighter pilot, Franz Stigler, took off to finish it. Pulling up behind the bomber, he saw the shattered fuselage and the wounded men inside and the dead tail gunner, and he did not fire. He later said that shooting them would have been like shooting a man in a parachute. Instead he flew close alongside, tried to signal Brown to land in Germany or fly to neutral Sweden, and finally escorted the bomber past German flak positions over the coast. Then he saluted and turned away. Brown nursed the plane back to England.

Neither man spoke of it for decades. In 1990 Brown, searching for the German pilot, placed a notice in a newsletter for former fighter pilots. Stigler, then living in Canada, answered. They met, became close friends, and both died in 2008.
lesson: Mercy toward someone who is helpless, even when you are told he is your enemy, keeps you human. It can also create a bond that outlives the conflict itself.
location: Over northern Germany and the North Sea coast
source: Adam Makos with Larry Alexander, A Higher Call (2012); interviews with both men
